In [[mathematics]], in [[semigroup theory]], a '''Rees factor semigroup''' (also called '''Rees quotient semigroup''' or just '''Rees factor'''), named after [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]], is a certain [[semigroup]] constructed using a semigroup and an [[ideal of a semigroup|ideal of the semigroup]].

Let ''S'' be a [[semigroup]] and ''I'' be an ideal of ''S''. Using ''S'' and ''I'' one can construct a new semigroup by collapsing ''I'' into a single element while the elements of ''S'' outside of ''I'' retain their identity. The new semigroup obtained in this way is called the '''Rees factor semigroup of ''S'' modulo ''I'' ''' and is  denoted by ''S''/''I''.

The concept of Rees factor semigroup was introduced by [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]] in 1940.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rees|first1=D.|authorlink1=David Rees (mathematician)|date=1940|title=On semigroups|journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]|volume=36|issue=4 |pages=387&ndash;400 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100017436 |s2cid=123038112 }} MR 2, 127</ref><ref>{{Cite book | last1=Clifford | first1=Alfred Hoblitzelle | author1-link=Alfred H. Clifford | last2=Preston | first2=Gordon Bamford | author2-link=Gordon Preston | title=The algebraic theory of semigroups. Vol. I | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | location=Providence, R.I. | series=Mathematical Surveys, No. 7 | isbn=978-0-8218-0272-4 |mr=0132791 | year=1961 }}</ref>

==Formal definition==
A [[subset]] <math>I</math> of a semigroup <math>S</math> is called an ''ideal'' of <math>S</math> if both <math>SI</math> and <math>IS</math> are subsets of <math>I</math> (where <math>SI = \{sx \mid s \in S \text{ and } x \in I\}</math>, and similarly for <math>IS</math>). Let <math>I</math> be an ideal of a semigroup <math>S</math>. The relation <math>\rho</math> in <math>S</math> defined by

: ''x'' &rho; ''y'' &nbsp;⇔&nbsp; either ''x'' = ''y'' or both ''x'' and ''y'' are in ''I''

is an equivalence relation in <math>S</math>. The equivalence classes under <math>\rho</math> are the singleton sets <math>\{x\}</math> with <math>x</math> not in <math>I</math> and the set <math>I</math>. Since <math>I</math> is an ideal of <math>S</math>, the relation <math>\rho</math> is a [[semigroup congruence|congruence]] on <math>S</math>.<ref>Lawson (1998) ''Inverse Semigroups: the theory of partial symmetries'', page 60, [[World Scientific]] with [https://books.google.com/books?id=2805q4tFiCkC&pg=PA60 Google Books link]</ref> The [[quotient semigroup]] <math>S/{\rho}</math> is, by definition, the ''Rees factor semigroup'' of <math>S</math> modulo
<math>I</math>. For notational convenience the semigroup <math>S/\rho</math> is also denoted as <math>S/I</math>. The Rees factor
semigroup<ref>{{citation|last= Howie|first= John M.|author-link=John Mackintosh Howie|title=Fundamentals of Semigroup Theory|year=1995|publisher=[[Clarendon Press]]|isbn=0-19-851194-9}}</ref> has underlying set <math>(S \setminus I) \cup \{0\}</math>, where <math>0</math> is a new element and the product (here denoted by 
<math>*</math>) is defined by

<math>s * t = \begin{cases} st & \text{if } s, t, st \in S \setminus I \\
0  & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}</math>

The congruence <math>\rho</math> on <math>S</math> as defined above is called the ''Rees congruence'' on <math>S</math> modulo <math>I</math>.

==Example==

Consider the semigroup ''S'' = { ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'', ''e'' } with the binary operation defined by the following Cayley table:

Let ''I'' = { ''a'', ''d'' } which is a subset of ''S''. Since

:''SI'' = { ''aa'', ''ba'', ''ca'', ''da'', ''ea'', ''ad'', ''bd'', ''cd'', ''dd'', ''ed'' } = { ''a'', ''d'' } &sube; ''I'' 
:''IS'' = { ''aa'', ''da'', ''ab'', ''db'', ''ac'', ''dc'', ''ad'', ''dd'', ''ae'', ''de'' } = { ''a'', ''d'' } &sube; ''I''

the set ''I'' is an ideal of ''S''. The Rees factor semigroup of ''S'' modulo ''I'' is the set ''S''/''I'' = { ''b'', ''c'', ''e'', ''I'' } with the binary operation defined by the following Cayley table:

| &nbsp; ''I''
| &nbsp; ''I''
|}

==Ideal extension==

A semigroup ''S'' is called an ideal extension of a semigroup ''A'' by a semigroup ''B'' if ''A'' is an ideal of ''S'' and the Rees factor semigroup ''S''/''A'' is isomorphic to ''B''. 
<ref>{{Cite book | last1= Mikhalev | first1=Aleksandr Vasilʹevich| last2=Pilz | first2=Günter|  title=The concise handbook of algebra| publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] | isbn=978-0-7923-7072-7 | year=2002 }}(pp.&nbsp;1&ndash;3)</ref>

Some of the cases that have been studied extensively include: ideal extensions of [[completely simple semigroup]]s, of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] by a [[completely 0-simple semigroup]], of a [[commutative semigroup]] with [[cancellation semigroup|cancellation]] by a group with added zero. In general, the problem of describing all ideal extensions of a semigroup is still open.<ref>{{SpringerEOM| title=Extension of a semi-group | id=Extension_of_a_semi-group | oldid=17640 | first=L.M. | last=Gluskin }}</ref>
